source: Boroditsky (2001) Does language shape thought? Mandarin and English speakers' conceptions of time
finding: Founding claim of the time-space line. English talks about time mostly as horizontal (ahead/behind). Mandarin also uses vertical shang (up, earlier) and xia (down, later). The paper says this habit shows up in implicit reaction times, even when Mandarin speakers work in English.
numbers: Exp 1: 26 English and 20 Mandarin speakers at Stanford; Mandarin speakers began English at mean age 12.8. 64 trials: two spatial primes (horizontal or vertical) then a true month-order question, 5 s deadline, 7% of trials dropped.
quote: one's native language plays an important role in shaping habitual thought
limits: Weaker Whorf, not determinism. The paper itself says language 'does not entirely determine' thought.
agent_relevance: Background for how a verbal habit can bias a non-verbal speeded task. Maps to wording-priming of an LLM, not to training.

source: Boroditsky (2001) Does language shape thought? Mandarin and English speakers' conceptions of time - Exp 1 results
finding: English speakers answered time questions faster after horizontal primes. Mandarin speakers answered purely temporal earlier/later questions faster after vertical primes. For before/after questions both groups were faster after horizontal primes.
numbers: English: horizontal 2128 ms vs vertical 2300 ms, F(1,25)=13.76, p<.01. Mandarin earlier/later: vertical 2347 vs horizontal 2503 ms; before/after: horizontal 2340 vs vertical 2509 ms; prime x target F(1,19)=4.55, p<.05. Three-way prime x target x language F(1,44)=5.24, p<.05.
limits: Small samples (20 Mandarin). Effect is an interaction of two ~150 ms differences. Later studies failed to reproduce it (see January and Kako, Chen, Tse and Altarriba).
agent_relevance: A stored habit shows only when the target is phrased in neutral terms. Reminder that prompt framing effects show up in the unframed items.

source: Boroditsky (2001) Does language shape thought? Mandarin and English speakers' conceptions of time - Exp 2 age of acquisition
finding: Among 25 Mandarin-English bilinguals the vertical bias fell with earlier age of first English, not with years of English exposure. The pattern echoes critical-period results for grammar (Johnson and Newport 1989).
numbers: Mean vertical bias 54 ms. Age of acquisition vs bias r=.47, p<.01 (r=.50 without one outlier at 582 ms). Years of exposure r=.12, p=.29. Partial r controlling exposure=.52; controlling age, exposure r=.29, p=.17. Age and exposure correlated r=.66.
limits: N=25, one outlier, correlational. Age of acquisition and exposure are confounded.
agent_relevance: Weak. Suggests timing of exposure matters more than total exposure, a point about humans only.

source: Boroditsky (2001) Does language shape thought? Mandarin and English speakers' conceptions of time - Exp 3 training
finding: A short lab training in vertical time talk (earlier = above/higher, later = below/lower) made 70 English speakers look like the Mandarin group. This was meant to rule out writing direction and other culture.
numbers: N=70 Stanford English speakers, 90 training questions. After training: earlier/later targets faster after vertical (2185 ms) than horizontal (2262 ms); before/after faster after horizontal (2040 vs 2156 ms). Interaction F(1,68)=10.25, p<.01; three-way with untrained group F(1,94)=5.65, p<.05. No difference between the two training wordings.
limits: Effect was temporary (minutes). The training is itself a priming manipulation, so it shows short-term metaphor priming more than a lifelong habit.
agent_relevance: Closest analogue to our setting: a few lines of metaphor in context change a later non-verbal judgment. Supports using in-context framing as a lever and also as a risk.

source: Lai and Boroditsky (2013) The immediate and chronic influence of spatio-temporal metaphors on the mental representations of time in English, Mandarin, and Mandarin-English speakers - Study 1
finding: Used the ambiguous 'move the meeting forward' question. English speakers mostly took the ego-moving reading (Friday). Mandarin speakers took time-moving (Monday). Mandarin-English bilinguals sat in between, tested in English.
numbers: Meeting question N=172: Friday 68.2% English (n=66), 38.2% bilinguals (n=55), 0% Mandarin (n=51); chi2(1,N=121)=9.7 p<.005 English vs bilingual. Mandarin proficiency predicts less ego-moving, beta=-0.250, Wald=10.4, p<.001. Clock question N=91: 2 pm answers 100% English, 41.0% bilinguals, 12.5% Mandarin; English proficiency beta=0.609, p<.01.
limits: Different testing sites (bilinguals in US, Mandarin monolinguals in Taiwan); test location was a significant predictor (beta=1.583, p<.05). After partialling, English proficiency still r(59)=.219, p<.05 one-tailed. Weak partial effect.
agent_relevance: Shows two-way effects of languages on interpretation of an ambiguous temporal instruction. For an agent, ambiguity in forward/back words is a real source of misreads.

source: Lai and Boroditsky (2013) The immediate and chronic influence of spatio-temporal metaphors on the mental representations of time in English, Mandarin, and Mandarin-English speakers - Study 2
finding: Within Mandarin, cueing with up-down metaphors made speakers lay out time on the vertical axis more; front-back cues made them use the sagittal axis more.
numbers: N=98 bilinguals (66 in California, 32 in Taiwan). Vertical arrangement 40% after up-down cues vs 19% after front-back, std beta=-0.255, p<.0001. Sagittal 24% vs 11%, beta=0.167, p<.05. Left-right not affected, beta=0.101, p=.15. Left-right axis 61% in California vs 36% in Taiwan (writing direction).
limits: Adjusted R2 only .06 to .07. Pointing task is explicit and scored by coders.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a metaphor in the prompt steers the spatial structure the reasoner uses at once.

source: Casasanto and Boroditsky (2008) Time in the mind: using space to think about time (as described in Bottini and Casasanto 2013)
finding: Psychophysics version of the metaphor claim. People watched lines of varied length and duration and judged one dimension. Distance leaked into duration judgments but duration did not leak into distance judgments. Six experiments with varied attention, memory and perception demands gave the same asymmetry.
numbers: Exact N and statistics not read in this session (only the summary in the 2013 paper). Direction: short lines judged shorter in time, long lines longer.
limits: Original paper not opened. The asymmetry is the evidence for Metaphor Theory over a symmetric magnitude system (ATOM).
agent_relevance: The asymmetry (time borrows from space) is a structural prior; an agent's duration reasoning may also lean on spatial wording.

source: Bottini and Casasanto (2013) Space and time in the child's mind: metaphoric or ATOMic?
finding: Tested the space-time asymmetry in children with a stricter control: the racing snails vanished at the end so neither space nor time stayed visible. Space still influenced time judgments more than the reverse in Dutch and Brazilian Portuguese children.
numbers: Dutch and Brazilian children, 18 trials each (12 interference, 6 control). Interference x target-dimension interaction: Dutch F(1)=16.53, p=.001, r2=.09; Brazilian F(1)=8.69, p=.003, r2=.05. No change with age (3-way F=0.42 and 1.91, n.s.) or language (F=0.30, n.s.). Group N not extracted here.
limits: Effect sizes small (r2 .05 to .09). The asymmetry is the same across these languages, so it is evidence for a general space-to-time dependence, not a language difference.
agent_relevance: The space-time map exists across languages: language adjusts it, does not create it.

source: Bottini and Casasanto (2013) Space and time in the child's mind: metaphoric or ATOMic? - ATOM vs Metaphor Theory framing
finding: Two accounts compete. A Theory of Magnitude (Walsh 2003): space, time, number share one analog magnitude system, so interference should be symmetric. Metaphor Theory (Lakoff and Johnson 1999): time and number depend asymmetrically on space, as language does.
numbers: No single number; the test is the direction of cross-dimension interference. Asymmetry reported in adults (Casasanto and Boroditsky 2008) and children (Casasanto 2010).
limits: Proponents of ATOM argue task artefacts (discriminability, persistent visible space cue). The 2013 study was built to remove one such artefact.
agent_relevance: Gives the two formal accounts we can use as vocabulary: one shared scale vs a space-to-X mapping.

source: Dolscheid and Casasanto (2015) Spatial congruity effects reveal metaphorical thinking, not polarity correspondence - Exp 1
finding: English speakers classified pure tones (262 Hz and 440 Hz, 400 ms) as high/low or front/back. A congruity effect (faster when high pitch paired with 'high') appeared for high/low but not front/back. So markedness alone is not enough.
numbers: 24 trials per condition, 48 per task. Congruity x space interaction t=|3.3|; congruity in high/low t=|4.5|; in front/back t=|0.2|. About 7% error trials and 6% outliers removed.
limits: t-values only; participant N for Exp 1 not extracted. English speakers only. Lab words, not natural talk.
agent_relevance: Control logic for any metaphor effect in an LLM: test with a matched but wrong spatial schema.

source: Dolscheid and Casasanto (2015) Spatial congruity effects reveal metaphorical thinking, not polarity correspondence - Exp 2 and Dolscheid 2013 summary
finding: Tall/short produced a congruity effect with pitch though English does not use tall/short for pitch. Big/small did not. This rules out polysemy and keeps the schema account. The paper also summarises Dolscheid 2013: pitch reproduction was pulled by line height in a continuous way, and Farsi speakers (thick/thin for pitch) were pulled by thickness, not height.
numbers: Exp 2 N=24 English speakers (1 replaced). Dolscheid 2013 detail (second-hand): nine line heights crossed with nine pitches; Dutch influenced by height not thickness, Farsi the reverse. Infants of 4 months sensitive to both mappings (Dolscheid 2014, second-hand).
limits: Dolscheid 2013 numbers were not read from the original. Infant result implies the adult language-specific mapping is a selection from an early shared set.
agent_relevance: Space-pitch is the cleanest example of a language-matched non-verbal bias. For an agent: an analogy built on a metaphor schema may be reached because of wording, not structure.

source: Dolscheid, Shayan, Majid, Casasanto (2013) The thickness of musical pitch: psychophysical evidence for linguistic relativity
finding: Dutch speakers say pitch is high/low; Farsi speakers say thin/thick (thin = high). Pitch reproduction was biased by irrelevant line height in Dutch and by line thickness in Farsi speakers. Verbal training in the other metaphor shifted the pattern.
numbers: Numbers not read (page not opened).
limits: Page not opened. A follow-up agent should pull the numbers.
agent_relevance: Best example of a Whorfian psychophysics effect with a trained-language manipulation, the closest human analogue to prompt framing.

source: Winawer et al. (2007) Russian blues reveal effects of language on color discrimination
finding: Russian has separate words for light blue (goluboy) and dark blue (siniy). Russian speakers were faster to tell two blues apart across the border than within a category. English speakers showed no such gain. A verbal dual task removed the advantage, a spatial dual task did not.
numbers: Abstract only read (body not in the open copy). Effect stronger for harder (closer) pairs. N and ms not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Shows that the language effect is online and can be knocked out by verbal load. For LLM prompting: an effect that depends on live verbal processing.

source: Pitt, Ferrigno, Cantlon, Casasanto, Gibson, Piantadosi (2021) Spatial concepts of number, size, and time in an indigenous culture
finding: Tsimane' adults in Bolivia, with little reading or counting culture, ordered number, size and time stimuli in space by magnitude, but with no consistent direction on any axis. Different domains went different ways within the same person.
numbers: Exp 2 N=60 Tsimane' adults aged 12 to 86, 3 domains x 3 axes. All three domains went the same direction in only 42% of cases (95% CI .32 to .54). Number-size same direction 80%, size-time 61%, time-number 53%. 12% of mappings excluded for wrong end identification. Perfectly ordered arrays 47 to 100% vs 1.5% by chance.
limits: Interpreter-mediated verbal instructions. Some near-zero mappings may reflect misunderstanding. Directions in industrial groups appear to come from reading, counting and similar practice, not language alone.
agent_relevance: Challenges the idea of one innate left-to-right magnitude line and the universal-ATOM account; supports direction coming from cultural practice.

source: Fedden and Boroditsky (2012) Spatialization of time in Mian
finding: Mian speakers in Papua New Guinea (river-based absolute spatial terms) laid out card sequences in three ways: left to right on the body, toward the body, or on an east-west landscape axis.
numbers: N=9 (13 to 55 years), 8 card sets, two sittings at about 145 degrees different facing. 6 of 9 body-relative (4 left-to-right at 0.99, 2 sagittal at 0.90); 3 of 9 absolute east-west. Years of schooling predicted left-to-right r(7)=0.61 and absolute r(7)=-0.65, both p<.05.
limits: N=9 only, the authors call the education link preliminary. Education and literacy are confounded with language exposure (Mian, Tok Pisin, English).
agent_relevance: Adds a case where the language's spatial frame (absolute) and the cultural writing frame compete; both show up.

source: Boroditsky and Gaby (2010) Remembrances of times east: absolute spatial representations of time in an Australian Aboriginal community
finding: Kuuk Thaayorre speakers arranged time cards from east to west regardless of facing direction, matching their absolute spatial language, while English speakers go left to right.
numbers: Numbers not read in this session; cited in Lai and Boroditsky 2013 and Fedden and Boroditsky 2012 as the source of the card task.
limits: Not opened. Small field sample, card task is explicit.
agent_relevance: An often-cited headline case for strong linguistic-spatial shaping of time.

source: Fuhrman and Boroditsky (2010) Cross-cultural differences in mental representations of time: evidence from an implicit nonlinguistic task
finding: English speakers (left-to-right writing) responded fastest with earlier on the left and Hebrew speakers (right-to-left) the reverse. Used as the main evidence that writing direction organizes the time line.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened. Writing direction, not spoken language.
agent_relevance: Warns that cultural artifacts, not only vocabulary, create the effects.

source: January and Kako (2007) Re-evaluating evidence for linguistic relativity: reply to Boroditsky (2001)
finding: Reported failure to replicate the English-speaker effect of Boroditsky (2001), and argued the original depended on specific item and procedural details.
numbers: Not read. I cannot give exact N or stats.
limits: Not opened; summarised from the citation record. Boroditsky and colleagues disputed it in later work.
agent_relevance: A failed replication of the headline time-metaphor result; treat the 2001 reaction-time effect as fragile.

source: Chen (2007) Do Chinese and English speakers think about time differently? Failure of replicating Boroditsky (2001)
finding: Reported no reliable Mandarin vertical bias with Boroditsky's paradigm; Chinese and English speakers did not differ as claimed.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; title and conclusion from citation record only.
agent_relevance: Second failed replication of the original RT result.

source: Tse and Altarriba (2008) Evidence against linguistic relativity in Chinese and English: a case study of spatial and temporal metaphors
finding: Another non-replication: similar priming tasks, no Mandarin vertical advantage.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Adds weight to the null-replication cluster.

source: Casasanto, Boroditsky et al. (2004) How deep are effects of language on thought? Time estimation in speakers of English, Indonesian, Greek, and Spanish
finding: Greek and Spanish use much/little for time; English and Indonesian use long/short. Speakers' duration estimates were biased by space or by quantity in line with their metaphor.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; may be a conference abstract. Details not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Early form of the idea that wording metaphors map to non-verbal estimation.

source: Casasanto (2016) Linguistic relativity (Routledge Handbook of Semantics)
finding: Splits relativity into effects of thinking for speaking and effects beyond language use, called Whorfian psychophysics; says evidence for the latter is strongest where tasks are non-verbal and implicit.
numbers: Not read; the SUBFIELDS summary cites it as the key work.
limits: Not opened; chapter text not available to this agent.
agent_relevance: Background framing of the field; lens for what could transfer to an LLM that only reads words.

source: Gurnee and Tegmark (2024) Language models represent space and time
finding: Linear probes on Llama-2 and Pythia activations recover real-world location and date from entity names across scales. Representations plateau around the model midpoint and improve with scale. They find single space and time neurons.
numbers: R2 at 60% depth, Llama-2-70b linear: world 0.911, USA 0.864, NYC 0.359, historical figures 0.835, entertainment 0.885, headlines 0.746. Llama-2-7b linear: world 0.881, USA 0.799, NYC 0.219, historical 0.785, entertainment 0.788, headlines 0.564. MLP probes add little.
limits: Tests geography and dates, not the human space-time metaphor asymmetry. The probe shows linear information, not use. Pythia far weaker than Llama (300B vs 2T tokens).
agent_relevance: LLMs hold an explicit linear time and space axis; this supports treating them as having a built-in space-time scaffold, with no evidence for the human asymmetry.

source: Abdou, Kulmizev, Hershcovich et al. (2021) Can language models encode perceptual structure without grounding? A case study in color
finding: Text-only models' color-term embeddings align with CIELAB perceptual space. Warm colors align better than cool. Larger models align better.
numbers: RSA Kendall tau on 18 terms: ELECTRA max about 0.33; other settings roughly 0.16 to 0.26 max (layer means near 0.01 to 0.2); linear-mapping selectivity max about 0.74 to 0.78; shuffled-centroid control non-significant (p>0.05). Table was garbled in extraction so cell values are approximate.
limits: Color terms, English. Weak means across layers. The paper does not test any human language-specific category effect.
agent_relevance: Evidence that perceptual structure can be partly learned from text; relevant to whether Winawer-type category effects could appear in an LLM.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the shadow of Babel: how language shapes reasoning in LLMs
finding: BICAUSE: aligned English and Chinese causal chains in forward and reversed order. A Qwen model attended more to causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, and did worse on reversed chains, especially in Chinese.
numbers: Qwen1.5-1.8B-Chat average accuracy 91.0% English and 91.2% Chinese on forward chains; English reversed 88.5%; Chinese reversed 76.5%. Layerwise attention similarity (SVCCA) fell with the same ordering.
limits: Single small model for the headline; no human data in the paper. Reversed Chinese chains are unusual text, so the drop may be a frequency effect, not a thought effect. Not a time-space test.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of language habit shaping reasoning: word-order priors travel into performance. Another reason to phrase tasks in the typical order.

source: Wang, Qin, Liu (2026) Where meanings converge and diverge: linguistic relativity across 81 languages
finding: Compared relations among 196 basic concepts across 81 languages using mBERT and XLM-R-large embeddings. Sociocultural meanings correspond more across languages than nature-and-motion meanings. Relational difference grows with geographic and genealogical distance.
numbers: Mean RSA dissimilarity Socio-Cultural vs Nature and Motion: .883 vs .921 (mBERT), .938 vs .973 (XLM-R-large). Contrast N&M minus Socio-Cultural .0375 (95% CrI .0345 to .0405) mBERT, .0346 (.0316 to .0376) XLM-R.
limits: Static lexical embeddings, not behaviour. Cross-model agreement is partial (the middle-domain order changes by model). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Shows a mixture: universal and language-specific structure inside the same models. Weakly relevant: embedding spaces are not pure translations of each other.

source: Kann (2019) Grammatical gender, neo-Whorfianism, and word embeddings: a data-driven approach to linguistic relativity
finding: Tested the Boroditsky et al. (2003) gender claim (key masculine in German, feminine in Spanish) on embeddings of 9 languages. Grammatical gender of inanimate nouns did not influence how nouns are used in context.
numbers: Nine languages, Wikipedia embeddings with window size 2; results reported as not supporting the neo-Whorfian claim. Exact accuracies not extracted.
limits: Only distributional text, not behaviour; absence in text does not rule out a human memory effect.
agent_relevance: A null result from text for a neo-Whorfian claim: not every human effect appears in text statistics.

source: Stanczak, Du, Williams, Augenstein, Cotterell (2023) The causal influence of grammatical gender on distributional semantics
finding: Found a link between a noun's grammatical gender and the adjectives used with it in Wikipedia, but when noun meaning is controlled the link shrinks to close to zero.
numbers: Five languages (German, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish, Hebrew); the causal mutual-information estimate drops to near 0 under noun-meaning control, with both word2vec and WordNet representations.
limits: Text corpora only, five languages; the causal model depends on the noun-meaning representation (WordNet gave lower values than word2vec).
agent_relevance: Method point: control the confounder (meaning) before claiming a language effect on thought. Useful for any wording-effect test on our agent.
